title: Born in Calamba
teaser: A house by the lake, and a mother who teaches
story: José Protasio Rizal Mercado y Alonso Realonda was born on 19 June 1861 in Calamba, a farming town on the shore of Laguna de Bay. He was the seventh of eleven children of Francisco Mercado and Teodora Alonso. The family lived in a two-storey bahay na bato near the town church: stone walls below, hardwood and capiz-shell windows above. Part of the ground floor opened to the street for Doña Teodora's small businesses. His mother was his first teacher. She taught him the alphabet when he was about three and read stories to him at night. One story was about a young moth that flew too close to a lamp's flame. Rizal remembered it all his life. From the house he could see Mount Makiling, the mountain that watches over Calamba.

title: School in Biñan
teaser: First formal school, away from home
story: In June 1869 Paciano took his younger brother José, then eight, to the town of Biñan to go to school. Classes were held in the house of the teacher, Maestro Justiniano Aquino Cruz, a small nipa house near the home of their aunt. Rizal later described him as tall and thin, strict, and very learned in Spanish and Latin grammar. On his first day José was teased, got into a fight with the teacher's son Pedro, and won. He was punished with the ruler more than once, but he soon led the class. An old painter, Juancho Carrera, also taught him to draw and paint. Near the end of 1870 a letter called him home, and he sailed back to Calamba on the steamer Talim. Years later he wrote about the tears he shed on leaving Calamba for Biñan.

title: First day at the Ateneo
teaser: A small boy, a big school, two rival "empires"
story: In June 1872, eleven-year-old José went to Manila to enter the Ateneo Municipal, a school run by Jesuit priests inside the walls of Intramuros. At first the school turned him away. He had registered late, and he looked small and sickly. With help from Manuel Xerez Burgos, he was accepted. The Jesuits split each class into two rival ‘empires’, Romans and Carthaginians, who competed for the top places. José began at the bottom and rose to ‘emperor’ within a month. He studied Spanish, Latin, mathematics and the sciences, and he began writing poems. In March 1877 he finished with a Bachelor of Arts and the highest grades, called sobresaliente. Years later he said his time at the Ateneo shaped how he thought and worked.

title: University in Intramuros
story: In 1877 Rizal entered the University of Santo Tomas, run by Dominican friars inside the walls of Intramuros. He first took philosophy and letters, then in 1878 he moved to medicine, partly because his mother's eyes were failing. He did not enjoy the school. He later wrote that the Dominican teachers were hostile to Filipino students and that the teaching was old-fashioned. Outside class he did well. In 1879 the Liceo Artístico-Literario of Manila held a poetry contest for native and mestizo writers. Rizal, eighteen, won first prize with "A la juventud filipina", a poem calling the Filipino youth the "fair hope" of the motherland. His prize was a silver pen shaped like a feather. In May 1882 he quietly left to finish his studies in Spain.

title: Arriving in Spain
story: Rizal left Manila secretly on 3 May 1882. Only his brother Paciano and a few relatives knew. After a sea voyage through Singapore, the Suez Canal and Marseille, he reached Barcelona on 16 June 1882. He stayed at the Fonda de España and walked the Rambla, the city's long, tree-lined avenue. At first he thought the city ugly, but within weeks he changed his mind and came to like it. In Barcelona he wrote "Amor Patrio" (Love of Country), his first essay written abroad. It was published in Manila on 20 August 1882 in the newspaper Diariong Tagalog, under the pen name Laong Laan, in Spanish with a Tagalog translation by Marcelo H. del Pilar. In the autumn he moved to Madrid to study medicine.

title: Student in Madrid
teaser: Two degrees at once, far from home
story: On 3 May 1882, Rizal left Manila for Spain without telling his parents; only his brother Paciano and a few relatives knew. After arriving in Barcelona, he moved to Madrid and enrolled at the Universidad Central, the country’s leading university, on Calle de San Bernardo. He took two courses at once: medicine, and philosophy and letters. He also studied painting and languages in his spare time. Money from home was often late, so he lived simply. In 1884 he finished his licentiate in medicine, and in 1885 his licentiate in philosophy and letters. In Madrid he joined other Filipino students who wanted reforms in the Philippines. At a banquet in 1884 he gave a famous toast honouring the painters Juan Luna and Félix Resurrección Hidalgo.

title: Training as an eye doctor
story: After finishing his medical studies in Madrid, Rizal went to Paris to train as an eye doctor. He chose this field because he wanted to cure his mother's failing eyesight. From November 1885 to February 1886 he worked as an assistant to Dr. Louis de Wecker, one of the leading eye surgeons in France. In the clinic he watched operations and learned to do them himself. He wrote home that he could now perform all the operations, though they needed a lot of practice. In his free time he visited Filipino friends, among them the painter Juan Luna and the Pardo de Tavera family. Paris was expensive, and he lived carefully. On 1 February 1886 he left for Germany to continue his training.

title: Spring in Heidelberg
teaser: An eye clinic and a poem to flowers
story: Rizal arrived in Heidelberg, an old university town on the Neckar River, on 3 February 1886. He worked at the university eye clinic under Professor Otto Becker and attended lectures there. Because he already held a Spanish medical licence, he was allowed to observe and assist even though he was not enrolled. German students liked him, partly because he played chess well. In spring, flowers bloomed along the river, among them his favourite, the light-blue forget-me-not. Homesick, he wrote the poem "A las flores de Heidelberg" (To the Flowers of Heidelberg), asking the flowers to carry his love home. On 31 July 1886, from Heidelberg, he wrote his first letter to Ferdinand Blumentritt, an Austrian teacher who studied the Philippines. It began a friendship that lasted the rest of his life.

title: A village in the hills
story: In the spring of 1886 Rizal went to stay in Wilhelmsfeld, a village in the wooded hills above Heidelberg. He lived for about three months in the vicarage of the Protestant pastor Karl Ullmer, with the pastor's wife and their children Etta and Fritz. Rizal was a Catholic, but he and the pastor became close friends. They talked often about religion and found they agreed on many things. The quiet village helped him work. Here he wrote the last chapters of his first novel, Noli Me Tangere. His German also improved. On 25 June 1886 he returned to Heidelberg. Today the village remembers him with a park named after him.

title: Leipzig
story: Rizal arrived in Leipzig, a city of books and printers, on 14 August 1886. He attended lectures at the University of Leipzig and made friends with scholars there. Life was cheaper than in Heidelberg, and he earned some money correcting proofs for a publishing house. He also worked on translations into Tagalog. One was Friedrich Schiller's play Wilhelm Tell, the story of a Swiss hero who stood up to unjust rulers, so that Filipinos could read about a fight for freedom. Another was a set of fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen, for his nieces and nephews. Historians do not fully agree on where each translation was started and finished. On 29 October 1886 he left Leipzig for Dresden, and then went on to Berlin.

title: The Noli is printed
story: Rizal arrived in Berlin in late 1886 to continue his medical training and finish a novel he had been writing for years: Noli Me Tangere. The book showed the abuses Filipinos suffered under Spanish rule, through the story of Crisóstomo Ibarra. By the time it was done, Rizal had almost no money left and nearly gave up. Then his friend Dr. Maximo Viola, a fellow Filipino from Bulacan, came to visit. Viola lent him the money to print it. In March 1887, the first 2,000 copies came off the press in Berlin. Rizal sent copies to friends, including Ferdinand Blumentritt. The novel spread quietly to the Philippines, where the Spanish authorities banned it. It made Rizal famous, and a target.

title: Meeting Blumentritt
story: Rizal and Ferdinand Blumentritt had written to each other for almost a year, but they had never met. In May 1887, after the Noli was printed, Rizal and his friend Maximo Viola set out on a tour of Europe. On 13 May 1887 their train reached Leitmeritz in Bohemia, then part of Austria-Hungary, and Blumentritt was waiting at the station. He helped them find a room at the Hotel Krebs and took them home to meet his wife Rosa and their children. For four days he showed them his town, its beer gardens and its old square. On 16 May 1887 Rizal and Viola signed the city's memorial book after meeting the mayor. The two friends met only this once, but they wrote to each other until the night before Rizal died.

title: Home again
story: Rizal came home in August 1887 after five years in Europe. His ship reached Manila on the night of 5 August, and on 8 August he was back in Calamba. He turned the ground floor of the family house into a clinic. His first patient was his mother, whose eyes were clouded by cataracts. News spread that a doctor from Germany had arrived, and patients came from far away. People called him "Doctor Uliman", from alemán, German. But the Noli had angered powerful people. The Governor-General called him to Malacañang and gave him a Spanish officer as a bodyguard. Rizal also helped the farmers of Calamba prepare a report on their troubles with the Dominican estate that owned their land. To protect his family, he left again on 3 February 1888.

title: Spring in Japan
story: Rizal reached Yokohama on 28 February 1888 and went on to Tokyo. The Spanish Legation in Azabu invited him to stay as its guest, which also let the Spanish keep an eye on him. He stayed about six weeks. He studied the Japanese language and learned enough to get by, watched kabuki theatre, and filled a notebook with sketches. He admired how clean and honest the country was, but disliked seeing men pull other people in rickshaws. He became close to Usui Seiko, called O-Sei-san, who showed him the city and helped him with the language. He thought for a while of staying, but his work for his country came first. On 13 April 1888 he sailed from Yokohama on the steamer Belgic, bound for America.

title: Across America
story: The Belgic reached San Francisco on 28 April 1888, but the passengers were not allowed to land. The ship was held in quarantine because of a smallpox scare, though no one on board was sick. Rizal suspected the real reason was politics: there were hundreds of Chinese workers on board, and the United States was then passing laws to keep Chinese workers out. He landed on 4 May and stayed two days at the Palace Hotel. On 6 May he took the ferry to Oakland and boarded a train across the continent, through Sacramento, Reno, Omaha, Chicago and Albany. He reached New York on 13 May. He admired America's size and wealth but wrote that it did not give equal freedom to people of all races. On 16 May he sailed for Liverpool on the City of Rome.

title: The British Museum
teaser: Annotating an old history of the islands
story: Rizal arrived in London in late May 1888 and stayed for most of a year. He rented two rooms from the Beckett family at 37 Chalcot Crescent, Primrose Hill. A blue plaque on the house remembers him today. He came to London for one reason: the British Museum. Its Reading Room, under a great dome, held rare books about the Philippines that he could not find elsewhere. Day after day he copied by hand a history of the islands written in 1609 by Antonio de Morga, a Spanish official. He added his own notes to show that Filipinos had a culture, trade and writing before the Spanish arrived. In March 1889 he moved to Paris, where the book would be published.

title: Paris, 1889
story: Rizal moved to Paris in March 1889, the year of the Exposition Universelle, a world's fair held from May to October. Its star was the brand-new Eiffel Tower. Rizal gathered his Filipino friends in Paris into a club. They first called it the Kidlat Club, because it would last only as long as the fair, like lightning. Then, after seeing Native Americans riding proudly in Buffalo Bill's show, they renamed themselves the Indios Bravos, the Brave Indios. Spaniards used 'indio' as an insult; Rizal wanted his friends to wear it with pride and to excel in study and sport. He also finished his annotated edition of Morga's history. It was printed in Paris by Garnier Hermanos in 1890.

title: Brussels
story: Paris was costly and full of parties, so early in 1890 Rizal moved to Brussels to save money and write. He lodged in a boarding house run by two sisters, Suzanne and Marie Jacoby, at 38 Rue Philippe de Champagne. There he worked on his second novel, El Filibusterismo, and wrote articles for La Solidaridad, the Filipino reformists' newspaper. His longest essay, "Sobre la indolencia de los filipinos" (On the Indolence of the Filipinos), appeared in five parts from July to September 1890. In it he argued that Filipinos were not lazy by nature, and that the troubles of colonial rule had taught them to stop working hard. That year brought bad news from home: the estate dispute in Calamba was going against his family.

title: Biarritz
story: In February 1891 Rizal went to Biarritz, a resort town on the Atlantic coast of France, to rest after a hard year. He stayed as a guest of the Boustead family, old friends, at their winter house, the Villa Eliada. There he grew close to their daughter Nellie. He hoped to marry her, but it did not work out: she wanted him to become a Protestant, and her mother did not favour the match. They parted as friends. Rizal turned back to his writing. On 29 March 1891, the eve of his departure for Paris, he finished the manuscript of El Filibusterismo. He wrote to Blumentritt that day: "I have finished my book!"

title: El Filibusterismo
story: On 5 July 1891 Rizal moved to Ghent, a Belgian university city where printing was cheaper. He found a printer, F. Meyer-Van Loo on Vlaanderenstraat, who would print El Filibusterismo and accept payment in parts. Money soon ran out. Rizal pawned his jewels, lived on very little food, and printing stopped halfway. He even thought of burning the manuscript. Then his friend Valentín Ventura in Paris heard of his trouble and sent money, and the work went on. On 18 September 1891 El Filibusterismo came off the press. Rizal dedicated it to Gomez, Burgos and Zamora, the three priests executed in 1872. He sent the first copies to friends in Hong Kong and gave the original manuscript to Ventura.

title: Hong Kong
teaser: An eye clinic and plans for home
story: Rizal left Europe and reached Hong Kong, then a British colony, on 20 November 1891. He opened an eye clinic at No. 5 D'Aguilar Street in Central and soon had many patients, Chinese, British and Portuguese among them. His family, who had lost their lands in Calamba, joined him, and they lived together at No. 2 Rednaxela Terrace. Christmas 1891 was one of the happiest of his life. He operated on his mother's eye, and she could read again. He also made a plan to move Filipino families to North Borneo and start a farming colony there, but it came to nothing. In June 1892 he decided to go home to Manila, knowing it was dangerous. Today plaques mark both his clinic and his house.

title: La Liga Filipina
story: Rizal returned to Manila on 26 June 1892. On the evening of 3 July he met with Filipino patriots in the house of Doroteo Ongjunco on Ilaya Street, Tondo. There they founded La Liga Filipina, a society for peaceful reform. Its aims were to unite the whole country, to help members in need, to defend them against injustice, and to encourage education, farming and trade. Among those present was Andrés Bonifacio. Three days later, on 6 July, Rizal was arrested. The authorities said that leaflets attacking the friars had been found in his luggage. He was held in Fort Santiago and then sent into exile in Dapitan, in Mindanao, arriving on 17 July 1892. Soon after, Bonifacio founded the Katipunan.

title: Teacher in exile
teaser: Sent far from Manila, he builds for the town
story: In July 1892, days after founding La Liga Filipina in Manila, Rizal was arrested and sent into exile in Dapitan, a small town in Mindanao. He arrived on 17 July 1892. Soon after, he won a share of the government lottery and used it to buy land in Talisay, about a kilometre from the town. There he built houses of bamboo, wood and nipa. He opened a school for boys, who did chores and farm work instead of paying fees. He treated patients, and poor patients paid nothing. He built a water system for the town, drained marshes and lit the plaza. He also farmed, wrote poems and collected plants and animals for European scientists. He stayed four years.

title: Fort Santiago
story: In 1896 Rizal was allowed to leave Dapitan to serve as a volunteer doctor in Cuba. While he was at sea, revolution broke out in the Philippines. He was arrested on board, held in Barcelona, and shipped back to Manila, arriving on 3 November 1896. He was locked in Fort Santiago. On 26 December a military court tried him for rebellion, sedition and illegal association. He could not question the witnesses, and he was sentenced to death. On 29 December he was moved to the prison chapel. That day he finished a poem of fourteen stanzas, a farewell to his country. He hid it inside a small alcohol stove and gave the stove to his sister Trinidad, saying in English, "There is something inside." The poem is now known as Mi Último Adiós.

title: His final day
story: Early on the morning of 30 December 1896, José Rizal was taken from Fort Santiago and walked to Bagumbayan, the open field beside Manila Bay. There, at about seven o'clock, he was executed. He was thirty-five years old. His death did not end the struggle for freedom; it made it stronger. Within two years the Philippines declared its independence. The field where he died is now Rizal Park, also called the Luneta, and his monument stands there, guarded day and night. Every 30 December the country remembers him on Rizal Day. His novels, his poems, his letters and the places he lived are still with us, and so are the questions he asked about justice, education and love of country. This is the last stop on his journey.

lines.text: Bagumbayan, 30 December 1896. Here Rizal's journey ended.
